Palisades Disaster Recovery District Heads to City Council Committee in November

by Sophia Sleap October 19, 2026October 19, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:09
Instaread

A proposal to create a disaster recovery district for Pacific Palisades—potentially capturing between $325 million and $1.9 billion in tax increment funding for infrastructure and recovery projects—is headed to the City Council’s Budget and Finance Committee in November, according to representatives from Council District 11.

The Palisades Disaster Recovery District would enable future property tax growth in the Palisades to be put into a fund specifically for infrastructure and recovery projects, rather than having that revenue directed to the city’s general fund. The Ad Hoc Committee for L.A. Recovery passed the proposal on October 9, though the exact date of the council vote has yet to be confirmed.

The City Council must approve a resolution of intention before the second anniversary of the Palisades Fire on January 7 for the program to proceed, said Craig Bullock, planning director for Council District 11 at the October 15 Pacific Palisades Community Council meeting. The resolution does not mean that the City Council is obligated to create the district, he said.

Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park said at the meeting that she expects questions from the Budget and Finance Committee about what redirecting the money would mean for the city’s general fund, though she stressed that the disaster recovery district would be beneficial for the community.

“There are some real opportunities to use this money in a way that keeps it local in the Palisades,” Park said, “and for projects that you all as a community can and will identify as a priority for yourselves.”

Bullock said the sooner the Palisades recovers, the sooner the city’s budget will recover too.

“We can’t afford to have a recovery that drags,” he said.

If the resolution is approved, the next step would be to determine how the district would be governed, Bullock said. A public financing authority of at least five members—three elected officials and at least two community members—would lead it. Under state law, recovery district board members must live in, own property in or represent a business in the district. 

Several PPCC members said at the meeting that they needed to know who would govern the district before they could feel confident supporting its creation.

“I think it’s very important to the buy-in of everyone to understand the governance structure,” said Elissa Ashwood, PPCC representative for Area 3. “Specifically, who those people will be.”

Park urged community members to attend the City Council’s Budget and Finance Committee meeting, which is slated for either Tuesday, November 3, or Tuesday, November 24, at 2 p.m.

“This is where I am going to need your help organizing and advocating,” Park said. “It continues to be really important for my colleagues on the council to hear from you and why this matters.”

“It’s impactful to have lots of us come down to City Hall and go to the meeting and be supportive and speak publicly,” said Sue Kohl, chair emeritus of the PPCC.

The PPCC will schedule a special meeting within the next two weeks to decide its position on the disaster recovery district ahead of the Budget and Finance Committee meeting.

Senate Bill 782, signed into law in October 2025, allows cities and counties to establish disaster recovery districts. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a resolution of intention in November 2025 to create a recovery district for unincorporated Santa Monica Mountains communities affected by the Palisades Fire. 

The city of Los Angeles has not used tax-increment financing for disaster recovery since the 1994 Northridge earthquake, Bullock said. This means there is a “learning curve,” he said, and Park’s staff is meeting with other council offices to explain the benefits of the recovery district approach.

The five districts created after the 1994 earthquake—called Earthquake Disaster Assistance Projects—were set up within 11 months after the earthquake. Bullock said the City Council initially declined to fund the feasibility study for the Palisades that is required to set up a disaster recovery district, which delayed the process.

The PPCC will meet again on Thursday, November 12, at 6 p.m. The online meeting will feature an update from California State Parks.
